title: API Auth & Token Security: Quick Revision Notes
summary: Night-before revision notes on API keys, sessions versus tokens, JWT structure and pitfalls, OAuth 2.0 flows, scopes, refresh tokens and HTTPS.

chapters.title: API Keys, Sessions and Tokens
points: Authentication proves who you are (401 when it fails); authorization decides what you may do (403 when it fails)
API key: a long static secret that identifies a calling app, sent in a header such as 'X-API-Key: <key>' or 'Authorization: Bearer <key>', never in the URL
Session: the server stores state and gives the browser an opaque ID in a cookie, so logout or revoke is just deleting the server record
Token (stateless): the server signs a self-contained token and keeps no record, so it scales across servers but is hard to revoke before expiry
Comparison: API key = machine identity, long-lived, no user context; session = stateful, easy revoke, cookie-bound; token = stateless, short-lived, carries claims
Interview Point: Q1 401 vs 403? Q2 Why are sessions easier to revoke than JWTs? Q3 When is an API key the right choice over OAuth?

chapters.title: JWT Structure and Pitfalls
points: JWT = three base64url parts joined by dots: header.payload.signature; header holds alg and typ, payload holds claims
Standard claims: iss (issuer), sub (subject), aud (audience), exp (expiry, Unix seconds), iat (issued at), nbf (not before)
Signed is not encrypted: anyone can base64-decode the payload, so never put secrets or PII in it
Verify on every request: signature, exp, iss and aud; HS256 uses one shared secret, RS256 uses a private key to sign and a public key to verify

Pitfalls: accepting alg 'none', trusting the alg header instead of pinning it, algorithm confusion (RS256 key used as an HS256 secret), long expiry with no revocation, storing JWTs in localStorage where XSS can read them
Interview Point: Q1 Why is a JWT readable but tamper-proof? Q2 What is the alg=none attack and how do you stop it? Q3 HS256 vs RS256: when to use which? Q4 How do you revoke a JWT?

chapters.title: OAuth 2.0 Flows and Scopes
points: OAuth 2.0 is delegated authorization: a client gets limited access to a resource owner's data without the password; roles are resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server
Authorization Code + PKCE (web, SPA, mobile): redirect to /authorize, user consents, callback returns a code, client POSTs code and code_verifier to /token for an access token
PKCE: client sends code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)) up front and the verifier at exchange, so a stolen code is useless; use it for all public clients
Client Credentials: machine-to-machine, no user, client_id and client_secret go to /token; Implicit and Password flows are deprecated, do not use them

Scopes limit what a token can do (e.g. read:orders, write:orders), are requested in the scope parameter and approved by the user, and the resource server must enforce them on each call; the state parameter blocks CSRF on the redirect
Interview Point: Q1 Why is PKCE needed? Q2 Which flow for a backend job with no user? Q3 What does a scope do and who enforces it? Q4 Why was Implicit flow dropped?

chapters.title: Refresh Tokens and Token Lifecycle
points: Access token: short-lived (about 5 to 15 minutes), sent on every API call; refresh token: long-lived, sent only to the /token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token to get a new access token
Refresh token rotation: each use returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; reuse of an old one signals theft, so revoke the whole token family
Store refresh tokens server-side or in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie; never in localStorage or logs
Revocation: delete the refresh token on the server, and keep access tokens short because they stay valid until exp unless you keep a denylist or use introspection
Opaque vs JWT access token: opaque needs an introspection call to the auth server but is revocable at once; JWT is verified locally but valid until expiry
Interview Point: Q1 Why split access and refresh tokens? Q2 What is refresh token rotation and what does reuse detection do? Q3 Where should each token be stored?

chapters.title: HTTPS and Transport Security
points: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS, giving encryption, integrity and server authentication; without it any key, cookie or token on the wire can be sniffed
TLS handshake in short: client hello, server sends certificate, client validates the chain to a trusted CA and checks the hostname, both derive a symmetric session key, then data is encrypted with it
Certificate checks: a trusted CA signed it, the domain matches, it is unexpired and not revoked; never disable verification in code, for example verify=False
Cookie flags: Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (no JS access), SameSite=Lax or Strict (CSRF defence); send HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security) to force HTTPS and redirect HTTP to HTTPS
Never put keys or tokens in URLs or query strings, since they leak into logs, browser history and Referer headers; use the Authorization header
Interview Point: Q1 What does the TLS handshake achieve? Q2 What do Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite each stop? Q3 Why not send an API key in the query string?

chapters.title: Auth Cheat Sheet
points: Pick: API key for server-to-server identity; session cookie for first-party web apps; JWT or OAuth access token for APIs, SPAs and third parties
JWT checklist: pin alg, verify signature, exp, iss and aud, keep it short-lived, no secrets in payload
OAuth picks: Auth Code + PKCE for any user-facing client, Client Credentials for machines, never Implicit or Password
Tokens: access about 15 minutes, refresh rotated and stored HttpOnly, revoke on logout and on reuse detection
Always HTTPS plus HSTS; secrets in env vars or a vault, never in git or URLs; rotate leaked keys immediately
Interview Point: Q1 Walk through a secure login to API call end to end. Q2 What would you check first in a leaked-token incident? Q3 Sessions or JWTs for a new web app, and why?
